posts.author: sonicsuperadventure
posts.body:
Hello! I'm not quite sure this is the right place to ask but I'd assume so. I'm having trouble learning ruby scripting. I've tried to look for sites or videos, but I can't find anything. Specifically, I can't find the definition to these " reserved words ". This is the list of words I found while searching which go under this name:
BEGIN    class    ensure   nil      self     when
END      def      false    not      super    while
alias    defined? for      or       then     yield
and      do       if       redo     true
begin    else     in       rescue   undef
break    elsif    module   retry    unless
case     end      next     return   until
I've found the definition of " class " and " def ", but nothing on the other words. If someone could explain to me what they do and an example of what they'd be used for or a link with the information I desire it would be greatly appreciated. I don't want to use other people's scripts as I'd rather be able to make them myself.
Also, bonus question. Does it matter what I put after " def "? I've seen people either use " initialize " or " main " and I don't know if that means anything or not. Thank you for reading!
(I have no programming experience, if that matters)

posts.author: Timtrack
posts.body:
Hi !
The reserved words are keywords reserved to specific contexts in ruby. You do not need to know all of their purpose to code in ruby, just keep in mind that using them outside of their context will create errors in your code.
Since you have no knowledge of programming, I suggest you learn the basics with tutorials either in ruby or other simple languages like Python.
I've found this one online that seems decent:
https://www.learnrubyonline.org/
You will learn here how to display values, deal with variables and basic operations. Then you will see conditionnal branches (if/else) and loops (for, while...). You will deal with basic objects (Array and Hash tables) and finally will deal with methods (or functions).
When you are done with the basics, you can then consider learning about classes and modules.
If you want to rush into rpg maker scripting, you can also directly take some scripts (if you use VX Ace, I suggest Yanfly's) and look into the code and try to understand what they do.
While it is commendable to want to learn how to script to be able to do your own things, I suggest that you still take scripts online if they do what you aim for, it will save you plenty of time, you will even learn more things as you look into their code!
And feel free to ask questions in the forums, there are many knowledgable scripters around here.
Edit

sonicsuperadventure said:
Also, bonus question. Does it matter what I put after " def "? I've seen people either use " initialize " or " main " and I don't know if that means anything or not. Thank you for reading!
Click to expand...
def
comes from define, and it's a vital "command" for Ruby or else you'd end up with empty classes and modules that might or might not include CONSTANTS and @@class_variables.
Do you need a new method? Then go
def
ine it by selecting a name that will give you an idea on what it does.
You better learn what parent class / superclass & child class means before you use
super
.
If you know what
alias
means in Ruby, you pretty much know what
super
does in a class that has a parent class.
super
- calls the parent class's method at some point
alias
- calls the current class's original method at some point
This super class has to have defined the same method or
super
will fail.
alias
can be used as many times as you want but it only works in the current class and its child classes. Other child classes of its parent class will ignore it.
Just a weird example: class A with the laugh! method has child classes B and C. B modifies the laugh! method's behavior by laughing nervously, but C does not so it still laughs normally.
true
,
false
&
nil
are Ruby's boolean values. Well, nil isn't a true boolean value at all, yet, Ruby treats it as one for the sake of convenience. They're all used to test an object's truthy or falsey value, meaning that something IS real or IS NOT the case or IS NOT BECAUSE IT DOESN'T EXIST.
